context.guidance: Move credentials and keys that protect Personal Data out of source files and configuration into a secret store or the runtime environment. Rotate any value that has already been committed, and exclude .env and key files from version control and build context. Restrict the secret store to the identities that need it, as Rule 6(1)(b) requires for the systems that hold Personal Data.

value.fix: Delete the hard-coded signing key or secret from source and config files, and load it at runtime from a secret store (for example HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets Manager or GCP Secret Manager) or from an environment variable injected at deploy time, such as process.env.JWT_SIGNING_KEY or os.environ['JWT_SIGNING_KEY']. If the variable is missing, the app should refuse to start rather than fall back to a default. The value has already been committed, so treat it as compromised: generate a new key pair or secret, revoke the old one, and invalidate any tokens or sessions signed with it. Remove the value from git history with git filter-repo or BFG and force-push, and keep in mind that existing clones and forks still hold it. Add .env, .env.*, *.pem, *.key and similar key files to .gitignore and .dockerignore so they never reach version control or the build context. Commit a .env.example containing placeholder names only. Limit read access to the secret to the service identities that need it, using least-privilege IAM or Vault policies, and turn on audit logging, as Rule 6(1)(b) requires for systems that hold Personal Data. Add a secret-scanning check to pre-commit and CI (for example gitleaks or trufflehog) so this doesn't happen again.
